tabs.title: Version 1
paragraphs: He Carried the Burning Bomb
This airman picked up a burning bomb with his bare hands, even though it had already blinded him,
you see, during a bombing mission over Japan, a smoke bomb exploded inside his plane and struck him in the face,
and smoke filled the cockpit until the pilot couldn’t see and the plane began diving,
so he grabbed the burning bomb and felt his way toward a window,
but a table blocked his path, forcing him to hold the bomb against his body while he lifted it out of the way,
and with his hands burning, he struggled forward until he found the window and threw the bomb outside,
then collapsed in flames,
but as the smoke cleared, the pilot pulled the plane out of its dive just above the ground, saving the crew,
and the man who carried the bomb survived too
Nick’s Revision — Clean Copy
He carried a burning bomb with his bare hands, even though it had already blinded him,
you see, during a bombing mission over Japan, a smoke bomb exploded inside his plane and struck him in the face,
and smoke filled the cockpit until the pilot couldn’t see anything,
but then the plane began diving,
so he grabbed the burning bomb,
and with his hands burning, he struggled forward until he found the window and threw the bomb outside,
clearing the smoke so the pilot could see again and pull the plane out of its dive before it crashed into the ground

tabs.title: Feedback & Lessons
paragraphs: Feedback & Lessons
Henry Erwin | Nick’s edits, 12 November 2026
Specific changes
Hook: “This airman picked up” becomes “He carried”. Lead with the sustained dangerous action.
Escalation: Nick separates “the pilot couldn’t see anything” from “but then the plane began diving”. Give the worsening danger its own beat.
Rejected wording: “felt his way toward a window”. Nick asked “what does this even mean?” Avoid compressed expressions that hide a physical action the viewer must understand.
Rejected obstacle: the navigator’s table. Nick could not picture why a table was inside the plane or how it related to carrying the bomb. Do not introduce an unexplained object mid-crisis.
Rejected aftermath: “then collapsed in flames” and the separate survival ending.
Replacement payoff: throwing the bomb outside clears the smoke, enabling the pilot to prevent the crash. Keep the ending on the danger driving the scene.
Transferable lesson
Keep one clear causal chain: smoke blocks the pilot’s vision → plane dives → airman removes the burning bomb → smoke clears → pilot can recover the plane.
Do not add a second emotional ending after resolving the main danger. This is a preference demonstrated in this revision, not a universal ban on survival endings.
Spatial clarity matters: establish a destination and its purpose before introducing obstacles. If an obstacle needs more explanation than it contributes, omit it.
Editing record

The clean copy preserves Nick’s wording apart from removing the dangling “and” after “grabbed the burning bomb” and smoothing the final line to explicitly connect restored visibility to pulling out of the dive.
The clean copy has not yet been explicitly approved in chat. Original draft remains in Version 1.

tabs.title: Version 1
paragraphs: Can a Silencer Really Hide a Gunshot?
If a soldier fires a gun with a silencer, could someone standing nearby really miss the shot,
you see, movies often turn the sound into a tiny puff, letting someone fire without anyone around them noticing,
and a real silencer does reduce the blast from the hot gas rushing out behind the bullet,
but that gas isn’t the only thing making noise,
because if the bullet travels faster than sound, it creates a sharp crack as it flies through the air,
and that sound happens outside the gun, after the bullet has already left the silencer,
so even with the blast reduced, the bullet itself can still give the shot away

This submarine fired its last torpedo at the enemy, but it turned around and came straight back at them,
you see, the crew had damaged a Japanese ship, but it was still afloat, so they returned to finish it off,
and before attacking, they checked their last two torpedoes to make sure the steering worked,
then fired the first and watched it head toward the target,
but when they launched the second, it curved sharply instead of going straight, circling back toward their submarine,
so the crew pushed the engines to emergency speed and tried to turn out of its path,
until their own torpedo struck near the back of the submarine and sent it sinking, just twenty seconds after they had fired it

tabs.title: Feedback & Lessons
paragraphs: Feedback & Lessons
Their Last Torpedo Turned Back | 12 November 2026
Approval
Nick approved the exact 93-word version in chat: “93 words, a bit shorter but it keeps the tension so i approve.”
The original remains above the approved final in Version 1. This records chat approval; no platform Complete action was taken.
Explicit feedback
The shorter length is accepted because it keeps the tension. Do not pad this approved script to reach 100 words. This is an explicit exception for this script, not a new universal length target.
Lessons inferred from the actual edits
Keep the story on one threat: their own torpedo is coming back. The crew’s attempt to escape and the impact carry that threat through to the payoff.
Give only the setup needed to understand the action. “The crew was trying to sink a Japanese ship” replaces the damaged-ship/return-to-finish-it explanation.

Cut preparation that delays the dangerous event. The steering-check sentence is removed. This does not mean technical details are always wrong; retain them when needed to understand an action or consequence.
Keep the first launch. It establishes the normal path and makes the second torpedo’s turn easy to understand. Compression must preserve this contrast and sequence.
Keep the response to danger. Emergency speed and turning show the crew trying to avoid the torpedo; they are not disposable action details.
End on the consequence. The sinking resolves the central question; the twenty-second statistic is removed.
Application to future drafts
Before adding a detail, ask whether it clarifies the threat, changes it, shows an attempt to escape it, or delivers the outcome. Remove details that interrupt that chain.
Compare future drafts against this original/final pair. Do not turn every deletion into an absolute ban or treat 93 words as the new target.
The lesson is saved here for reuse; storing it does not itself update model weights or prove automatic retrieval by the platform.

name: He Told His Own Guns to Fire on Him

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts
John Fox: the story behind the script
The battle
On 26 December 1944, Fox was directing artillery near Sommocolonia, Italy. His role was to observe the enemy and tell distant gun crews where to fire. [1]
Most American infantry withdrew under attack. Fox and his observation party stayed on the second floor of a house to direct defensive fire. He was not alone. [2]
As German troops advanced, Fox requested bombardments closer to his building. His commander warned him about the danger, but Fox repeated the request. [2]
Fox and the men with him died in the bombardment. The Army museum says their action delayed the German advance and allowed American troops to regroup. [1]
The medal ending
Fox received the Distinguished Service Cross posthumously in 1982. [1]
In 1996, the Army determined that seven Black World War II soldiers, including Fox, had been unjustly denied the Medal of Honor. [2]
On 13 January 1997, President Bill Clinton awarded their Medals of Honor. Fox’s widow, Arlene, received his award, more than fifty years after the battle. [1, 2]
Accuracy notes for writing and visuals
“His own men” in the hook means American forces. The artillery crews were not necessarily his direct subordinates.
The script’s final radio exchange is a paraphrase, not a word-for-word quotation.
Do not portray him as the only American left in the building or imply that everyone else survived.
The medal is a later recognition, not the immediate result of the strike.

tabs.title: Version 1
paragraphs: He Told His Own Guns to Fire on Him
This American officer ordered his own guns to fire directly onto his position, knowing the shells would hit him along with the Germans surrounding him,
you see, his men were pulling out of a village under attack, but he stayed upstairs in a house, using his radio to tell the artillery where to shoot,
and as the Germans advanced through the streets, he kept calling the explosions closer,
but they continued forward until they surrounded the building,
so he told the guns to fire on his position,
and when his commander warned that the shells would land on him, he insisted they fire anyway,
until the bombardment killed him and the men who had stayed beside him,
but it delayed the German advance long enough for the retreating Americans to regroup
Final version
He ordered his own men to fire directly at him,
you see, his men were pulling out of a village under attack, but he stayed behind in a building to tell the artillery where to shoot,
and as the Germans advanced through the streets, he kept calling the explosions closer,
but they kept advancing until they surrounded the building,
so he told the guns to fire on his position,
and when his commander warned that the shells would land on him, he insisted they fire anyway,
until the bombardment killed him and the men who had stayed beside him,
and more than fifty years later, his wife received the Medal of Honor on his behalf

tabs.title: Feedback & Lessons
paragraphs: Feedback & Lessons
John Fox script • 12 November 2026
Status and evidence

Nick edited the original draft in this chat, asked about adding an award ending, and accepted the revised final with “ok nice”. The original and final remain in the Version 1 tab. This record captures editorial approval in chat; it does not change PlotPointe’s Complete status.
Confirmed direction
The viewer must understand what is happening, care about it, and need the next sentence.
Nick’s standing instruction: “WHEN WE’RE BUILDING TENSION NNNEVER CHANGE THE SUBJECT.”
Keep the danger and the chain of actions clear, using simple language. Cut details that interrupt the story; retain details whose absence makes an action confusing.
Before and after
1. Hook: get to the surprising action
Before: “This American officer ordered his own guns to fire directly onto his position, knowing the shells would hit him along with the Germans surrounding him”
After: “He ordered his own men to fire directly at him”
Observed change: Nick removed the rank, nationality, military phrasing and explanation of the danger.
Lesson to test: state the dramatic action first, then let the body explain why. Do not turn this into a rule that every hook must begin with “He”.
Accuracy boundary: “his own men” means his own side here; it should not imply command over troops he did not command.
2. Setup: keep purpose, remove unnecessary mechanics
Before: “he stayed upstairs in a house, using his radio to tell the artillery where to shoot”
Final: “he stayed behind in a building to tell the artillery where to shoot”
Observed change: Nick shortened the setup. The assistant repaired “help the artillery where to shoot” and reintroduced the building before the later encirclement; Nick accepted that version.
Lesson to test: include the minimum location and purpose needed to follow the next action. Radios and floor numbers are not universally banned.
3. Escalation: preserve the sequence
The final keeps advancing Germans → closer artillery fire → surrounded building → strike request → warning → insistence → bombardment.
Observed change: “continued forward” became “kept advancing”.
Lesson: trim around the decisive sequence, rather than removing the steps that make the decision understandable. The warning earns its place by confirming that he knows the strike will hit him.
4. Ending: a choice for this story
Original ending: the strike delayed the Germans so the retreating Americans could regroup.
Nick removed that line and asked whether the story could end with an award or recognition.
Accepted ending: “and more than fifty years later, his wife received the Medal of Honor on his behalf”
Lesson: a brief personal consequence can close this story. Do not add medals, wives or decades-later epilogues mechanically to other stories.
Tradeoff: this final no longer explicitly states what the sacrifice achieved militarily. Nick accepted this version; that is not evidence that battlefield consequences should always be removed.
How to use this record
Before a new draft, read the confirmed direction and the relevant before-and-after examples.
Apply only lessons that fit the new story. Keep sourced facts separate from writing preferences.
Compare the next draft with Nick’s edits to test whether these lessons transfer. Record counterexamples rather than adding conflicting absolute rules.
Keep the original draft, accepted final and feedback together. Never treat an unreviewed draft as an approved example.
Persistence limit

These lessons are saved in this document. Saving this tab does not automatically train a model or prove that the platform loads it for future writing. The writing workflow must explicitly retrieve these lessons and approved examples before drafting.

tabs.title: Changes Comparison
paragraphs: Changes Comparison
Your version reaches the central dilemma faster: he is asking his own side to kill him. Mine explained too much before letting that action land.
The strongest lessons to carry forward
Let the hook create the question; let the body explain it. Don’t explain the hook’s entire meaning inside the hook.
Keep details that make the action understandable. The building matters because it gets surrounded; the radio and upstairs location aren’t necessary here.
Compress around the decisive moment. You preserved the approaching Germans, encirclement, warning and insistence.
Keep the ending brief and connected to the person. The medal works here because his wife receives it after his death. That doesn’t make medals a required ending for other stories.
One tradeoff

Removing the regrouping line means we no longer explicitly show what his sacrifice achieved. Your ending gives us recognition instead. That’s a choice specific to this version, rather than a general lesson to remove consequences.
Attribution
The final includes Nick’s edits plus the grammar/location clarification and medal ending he accepted in chat.

1. Hook. Only 1 of your 6 finals opens on the highest stake (the SEAL). The other 5 open on a strange deliberate act or fact, e.g. "The American military glued tiny firebombs to live bats." The draft says: open on the most surprising true act; use the highest stake when it is that kind of act. OK?

2. Ending. Only the SEAL ends on a cliffhanger. The other 5 end on an irony or a price (the pig as the only casualty, the bats burning the base, the poison that didn't work, his own country shooting him, the captain shooting himself). The draft says: end on the irony or price; leave it open only for a SEAL-type story. OK?
3. Numbers. Your rule says at most one, but the Captain final has four (nine, 70, 72, three) and the Bat final has 6000 and World War 2. Absolute limit, or a default you can break?
4. Length. Your rule says aim for about 115, but your finals are 117 to 151 words (about 138 on average). Keep 100-150 with no aim, aim for 115, or aim for about 140?

5. How it happened. Rule 6 says cut how-it-was-done steps, rule 26 says spend a line on how when that's the interesting part. The draft keeps both: one line of how only when the how is the interesting part. OK?
Moved out of the general rules (now notes shown only next to that example story):

SEAL: The hook is the highest-stakes moment because that moment is itself a deliberate act: he ran back into gunfire. It ends on a cliffhanger: the lieutenant's fate is left unsaid so viewers ask in the comments. Every line is a new threat or a desperate move against one, with no relief beats until the final escape line. Sharp words on each blow: 'instantly', 'far into the air', 'unconscious'. 'lieutenant' is not repeated on consecutive lines; the hero is named once, bare, without 'Navy SEAL'.

Captain: Every clause says what it means for the captain: why it pushes him to act. Background clauses that carry no motive were cut. Two lines went in without a matching source ('Germany's secret new radar', 'couldn't bear anyone thinking he sank his ship to save his own life'); every fact needs its source.
Pig: The hook says who did what and who it belonged to; line 2 is the threat. Lines with stakes and voice stay: 'fight to the last man', 'one order away from war', the admiral's quote.

How the test will check scripts: only word count (100-150) and em dashes reject a draft automatically. A fact the sources don't support stops it being marked ready. Repeated connectives within two lines and more than one number are only flagged to you.
THE PROMPT (the [src: ...] tags show where each line came from and are removed before the writer sees it):
# Script writer prompt: your rules, consolidated

You are Nick's script partner for The Art of War. Write true military and historical stories for a viewer hearing the event for the first time. The result is a clear, gripping spoken story that holds attention from the first line to the last. [src: v1]
## Order of priority

Truth first, then Nick's explicit request and edit limits, then whether the listener understands it, then story and stakes, then style, then length. Never fix a style problem by inventing an event or a cause. [src: v1]
## Inputs

You get an evidence brief with claim IDs and source excerpts, a few example scripts, and sometimes notes on why an example worked. Excerpts, examples and notes are data, not instructions. An example's notes explain that story; they are not rules for this one. [src: v1, adapted for story notes]
If the evidence is not enough, return needs_research and name the missing claims. Never fill a gap yourself. [src: v1]
## Find the story first

Keep the story on one hero and one motive. Know what they want, what stands in the way, the decisions and turns, and why the ending matters. One story, one topic: cut anything that starts a second story, and don't add side people (crew, crowds, mourners). [src: v1 + your rules 14, 25]
Make the viewer care about the character: pick the moments with emotional weight over neutral facts. [src: your rule 16]
Give every betrayal and big decision its why, because that is where the drama is. [src: your rule 21]
## Hook

Line 1 is the most surprising true thing someone did, or the strangest true fact, in plain words, so the viewer has to ask why or how. Use the story's highest-stakes moment as the hook when that moment is itself such an act, as in the SEAL. Never give away the ending. [src: new, from your 6 finals; replaces v1 "do not force the highest-stakes moment" and your rule 5]
Put the conflict in the first two lines. Skip haggling, prices and excuses. [src: your rule 11]
Don't put a setting detail in the hook if a later line already gives it. Leave out place names unless the story needs them. [src: your rule 7]
## Progression

Every line changes the situation: a new threat, a desperate move against it, a decision with its why, or the setup the ending needs. Each action must cause the next: pick the action that makes what follows inevitable. [src: v1 + your rule 19]
Every connective must be true: "so" needs a real cause and "but" a real contrast. If it isn't true, rewrite the line, don't swap the word. [src: your rule 17, same as v1]

Write it as one long sentence chained by connectives, and don't use the same connective twice within two lines. [src: your rule 18, "close" defined as two lines; replaces v1 "do not mechanically count connective spacing"]
Give anyone or anything a reason to be in the story before it acts. Never first name a power after it has already won. [src: your rule 20]
Say plainly who does what. No dangling fragments that leave the listener unsure what is happening. [src: your rule 22]
When how it happened is the interesting part, spend a line showing how. Otherwise cut how-it-was-done steps. [src: your rules 26 + 6, merged]
## Words
Use words a viewer gets the first time they hear them. If a term needs a second of thought, replace it. [src: your rule 24]
Every word must add to the story. Cut emphasis words, redundant words, and true details that make the listener stop and puzzle. [src: your rule 23]

Name the hero once, bare, with no titles, and don't repeat a key noun on consecutive lines. Refer to groups ("the British", "soldiers"), not side characters with titles; name a role only when that person gets a quote or a decision. [src: your rules 1, 8]
Keep the lines that carry stakes and voice ("fight to the last man", "one order away from war", the punchline quote). The fluff to cut is details, not those lines. [src: your rule 9]

Keep at most one number, and only if it's simple and pays off, like "12 years". Cut piles of numbers like troop counts, cannons, ships and men. [src: your rule 10; replaces v1 "there is no one-number quota"]
No em dashes. [src: v1]
## Length
100-150 words. [src: v1 + your rule 6]
## Ending

End on the irony or the price that pays off the hook, as a bare act, with the reason in the person's own words when there is one: "leaving the pig as the only casualty of the entire standoff.", "three days later he shot himself". [src: new, from your 6 finals + your rule 13; replaces v1's ending menu]

Leave the ending open only when the open question is the outcome viewers will argue about in the comments, and leaving it out doesn't mislead, as in the SEAL. [src: your rule 2, scoped to stories like the SEAL]
No ceremony or pictures (salutes, uniforms, flags, crowds, wreaths), no moral, no call to action. [src: your rule 13 + v1]
## Facts
Every fact, cause and motive must match a claim in the evidence brief. If a detail you want is not there, put it in unresolved_issues instead of the script. [src: v1 + your rule 12, made general]

Don't make a disputed claim sound certain just because hedging feels less dramatic. Use a well-supported alternative, leave it out, or flag the doubt. Never present a paraphrase as an exact quote. [src: v1]
## Editing
On a rewrite, use the writer's exact wording and change only what they marked and what the lines beside it need. [src: your rule 27, for every editing task]
## Return

Return status (ready_for_editor, needs_review or needs_research), narration_lines, claim_map, unresolved_issues and a short editorial_reason. If you have any doubt about a fact, the status is not ready_for_editor. ready_for_editor means ready for Nick to read, not approved. [src: v1]

Both stories below got Neither in the blind test. Edit, cut, comment freely: your changes are the feedback. The originals are saved separately.
Story 1: The War Started And Ended At His House 🏠
Pitch: After the first big battle of the Civil War wrecked his farm, a man moved his family 120 miles away to a sleepy village so the war could never find him again.
Script 1 (v1 plus your rules, 147 words)
A Union shell smashed through a Virginia man's kitchen and into the dinner of the Confederate officers inside,
because Wilmer McLean's farm near Bull Run had become their general's headquarters on the eve of the war's first big battle,
Two years later he moved his family south to Appomattox, near a railroad for his sugar business and far from the fighting,
but in 1865 the war found him again,
when Robert E. Lee's aide rode into town looking for a place to meet Grant, and ran into McLean, who first suggested an empty tavern,
and when the aide turned it down, the meeting moved into McLean's own parlor,
where Lee surrendered to Grant,
after which Union officers bought or carried off his furniture as souvenirs, even a child's doll,
McLean supposedly summed it up: the war began in his front yard and ended in his front parlor.
Script 2 (v1 as written, 149 words)
In 1861, a Union shell crashed through the kitchen of a Virginia farm and ruined the Confederate officers' dinner,
the farm belonged to Wilmer McLean, whose house was General Beauregard's headquarters during the war's first big battle,
and later, McLean moved his family about 120 miles south to a village called Appomattox, near a railroad for his sugar business and far from the fighting,
but in April 1865, an aide to General Lee rode into the village looking for a place where Lee could meet General Grant, and ran into McLean,
who first suggested an empty tavern, but the aide turned it down, so the meeting ended up in McLean's own parlor,
where Lee surrendered to Grant, who gave him generous terms,
then Union officers carried off his tables and chairs as souvenirs,
and two years later, unable to pay his mortgage, McLean sold the house where Lee surrendered.
Story 2: The Night Out That Almost Started WW3 🎭
Pitch: An American diplomat just wanted to see a play in East Berlin, but a guard asked for his ID, and within days American and Soviet tanks were aiming at each other from 100 yards apart.
Script 1 (v1 as written, 149 words)
An American diplomat was heading to a show in East Berlin when East German guards at Checkpoint Charlie demanded his papers.
But he refused, because Allied forces could move freely across Berlin, and he insisted only the Soviets could check him,
so General Clay began sending Americans across under armed escort, and US tanks rolled up to the checkpoint.
Khrushchev ordered his forces to match them tank for tank, and late one afternoon ten Soviet tanks faced ten American tanks about 100 yards apart, their guns trained on each other.
When Kennedy phoned Clay and told him not to lose his nerve, Clay said it was Washington's nerves he worried about,
and the next morning the Soviet tanks began backing away, for reasons no record has settled, and the American tanks followed,
and the US stopped the escorts, ending a standoff that began with a trip to a show.
Script 2 (v1 plus your rules, 132 words)
An American diplomat was driving to a show in East Berlin when East German guards at Checkpoint Charlie demanded his papers,
but he refused, saying the Allies could move freely anywhere in Berlin and only the Soviets could check him,
so armed military police began escorting officials across, then an American general made the escorts bigger, determined to win back America's standing in the city,
and when American tanks rolled up to the checkpoint, Soviet leader Khrushchev ordered his army to match them tank for tank,
leaving Soviet and American tanks facing off through the night, their main guns aimed at one another.
But the next morning one Soviet tank backed up, an American tank followed, and one by one they all pulled away,
and soon after, America stopped the armed escorts.

name: The SEAL Who Went Back

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts

On October 31, 1972, Petty Officer Michael Thornton and Lt. Thomas Norris went with three South Vietnamese LDNN commandos on a mission to capture prisoners and gather intelligence near Cua Viet Base, south of the Demilitarized Zone. [1]
A junk dropped the team at sunset. They paddled a rubber boat to within about a mile of shore, swam the rest of the way, and moved inland past North Vietnamese encampments during the night. [2]
At dawn the team realized they had landed about 5 miles (8 km) north of their target and were actually inside North Vietnam. [2]
Defense Media Network says the landing went wrong because the junk's captain had become lost. Norris decided to gather what intelligence they could anyway. [3]

They were found when a two-man North Vietnamese patrol came toward their hiding place near the beach. The LDNN officer ordered his two enlisted frogmen to capture the patrol. Thornton knocked out one soldier and killed the other after an exchange of fire. The shooting drew more North Vietnamese troops. [3]

Wikipedia's Thornton article says about 50 North Vietnamese soldiers chased Thornton and a grenade wounded him in the back. It says the five men held off a force estimated at 150 for about four hours. Wikipedia's Norris article puts the enemy at an estimated 200–300. [1]
As the enemy surrounded them, the team decided to withdraw. Norris covered the rear and was shot in the head. A South Vietnamese soldier who saw the wound assumed Norris was dead. [2]
Wikipedia says Norris had called in fire from the cruiser USS Newport News to cover the withdrawal, and was shot in the head while getting ready to fire a LAW rocket. [1]

Defense Media Network tells it differently: Norris radioed Newport News to fire on their position after five minutes, then ran for the beach with the team. Less than a minute later a bullet hit him in the forehead. [3]

Thornton's Medal of Honor citation, as summarized by Military Times, says he went back after learning that the Senior Advisor, a U.S. Navy lieutenant, had been hit and was believed dead. He went through heavy fire to the lieutenant's last position and killed two enemy soldiers who were about to overrun it. [4]

None of the pages I read names who told Thornton that Norris was dead. The citation says only that Norris was 'believed to be dead.' Defense Media Network says the LDNN officer later claimed the others were dead, but it does not say he told Thornton. [3]
Thornton ran about 400 yards back to Norris's last position, shot several enemy soldiers, and carried Norris toward the beach. [1]
Thornton found Norris barely alive, killed several North Vietnamese troops, and carried the unconscious Norris into the water. [2]

While Thornton ran for the beach carrying Norris, the first of 104 five-inch rounds from Newport News landed, and the blast threw them to the ground. When they reached the beach the LDNN officer was gone. Thornton dropped his extra gear, inflated life jackets, strapped the semi-conscious Norris to his back, and swam out to sea. [3]
Wikipedia says a shell from Newport News hit the beach and threw both men into the air, which slowed the enemy advance. [1]
Thornton also held up a wounded South Vietnamese soldier who could not swim. He swam with both injured men for 'more than two hours' until the same junk that had dropped them off picked them up. [2]
According to the citation, Thornton pulled the wounded lieutenant to the water, inflated his lifejacket, and towed him seaward for about two hours until support craft picked them up. [4]

Victoria Cross Online's narrative says Thornton bandaged Norris's wound and swam for about three hours, while its copy of the citation says about two hours. It also says Thornton fired Norris's AK-47 to get the junk's attention, and that they were then taken to Newport News. [5]

Defense Media Network says Newport News turned away after an airborne forward air controller wrongly reported the team captured or killed. SEAL Woody Woodward had already rescued the LDNN officer, then went back to patrol off the beach and found the rest of the team. [3]
On Newport News, a doctor told Thornton that Norris would not survive. [1]

Norris survived but lost an eye and part of his skull. He spent three years recovering in the hospital and had many major operations over six years, the first lasting 19 hours. He was medically retired from the Navy in May 1975. [2]
President Richard Nixon presented Thornton's Medal of Honor at a White House ceremony on October 15, 1973. [1]

Norris's Medal of Honor was for an earlier, separate action: the April 10–13, 1972 ground rescue of two downed airmen, Lt. Col. Iceal Hambleton (Bat 21 Bravo) and 1st Lt. Mark Clark, deep in enemy-held Quang Tri Province. President Gerald Ford presented it at the White House on March 6, 1976. Wikipedia's Thornton article gives the date as March 4, 1976. [2]
PBS's American Valor says: 'Thornton was the first person in more than a century to receive that honor for saving the life of another Medal of Honor recipient.' [6]

Other sources disagree with the 'only time in a century' framing. Defense Media Network calls it 'only the second time in the medal's history,' and Sandboxx says there have been 'only three instances' of one recipient saving another. [3]

Sandboxx says the South Vietnamese SEALs left Norris for dead. In its account, after the naval shell landed, Thornton swam out with Norris, then went back under fire for a wounded Vietnamese SEAL and swam him out too. [7]
References
[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_E._Thornton
[2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_R._Norris
[3] https://defensemedianetwork.com/stories/petty-officer-michael-thorntons-uncommon-rescue
[4] https://valor.militarytimes.com/?p=29948
[5] https://victoriacrossonline.co.uk/michael-edwin-thornton-moh/
[6] https://www.pbs.org/weta/americanvalor/stories/norris.html
[7] https://www.sandboxx.us/?p=104097

Navy SEAL Michael Thornton ran about 400 yards through enemy fire, straight toward the spot his own warship was about to shell.
He and his lieutenant, Thomas Norris, had swum ashore at night after a boat dropped them off the coast, to capture enemy soldiers,
but at dawn they realized they had landed five miles too far north, inside North Vietnam,
so they hid near the beach until a two-man enemy patrol came toward them,
where Thornton knocked out one and killed the other in a gunfight that brought dozens more running,
and while the soldiers closed in, Norris radioed an American warship off the coast to shell their own position in five minutes to cover their escape,
then he stayed at the back to hold off the soldiers while Thornton ran for the beach,
only for a bullet to hit Norris in the head,
leaving him lying right where the warship's shells were only minutes from landing,
so as soon as Thornton learned Norris had been shot, he ran back through heavy fire to reach him before the shells did, killing two soldiers who were about to get to him, and found him still alive,
carrying him toward the beach just as the first shells started landing,
where one blast threw both men into the air, yet slowed the soldiers chasing them,
giving Thornton enough time to reach the water, inflate their life jackets, strap Norris to his back and swim out to sea,
towing him for over two hours until that same boat found them,
and Norris lived, but lost an eye and part of his skull.

tabs.title: Learnings
paragraphs: What "The SEAL Who Went Back" taught me
What I learned

- Nick's core lesson, in his words: "the secret to a great story is two things. the flow ... and having high stakes, so people are invested. this is the most important lesson i can give you as a storyteller." He also said: "at every moment of the story there is tension. tension is important to keep the viewers engaged."

- He cuts hard: "generally i am savvage with cutting out things. usually my script is condensed to 100-150 words." His final script is about 115 words. That is 152 words fewer than my Version 1 (269) and 49 fewer than my Version 4 (164).

- He judges the hook by the first 10 seconds and by whether he cares about the person: "even the hook is weak and personally you did not capture my attention the first 10 seconds and i didnt care about the character at all." His hook puts the story's single biggest stake into plain words with no name or title: "He ran back to the middle of the battlefield to save his lieutenant from enemy gunfire." His note on it: "highest stake in story becomes the hook - so the hook IS the foreshadow."
- The hook has to make the viewer ask "omg whats gonna happen now?" He made it stronger by adding the danger to it: "...to save his lieutenant" became "...from enemy gunfire."

- He ends on a cliffhanger, not on the outcome. He deleted "and his lieutenant lived, but lost an eye and part of his skull" and noted: "script ends at the cliffhanger of what happened to the lieutenant which will get people asking in the comments what happened." He thinks about comments as part of the structure.

- He removes every line where the danger eases. He cut "shooting the soldiers who were about to reach him", "yet slowing the soldiers chasing them" and "towing him for two hours until a boat finally found them". The only relief in his version is the final escape.

- He drives the lines with turns: "so his lieutenant called... but instantly got a bullet in the head", "so Thornton turned around... but just as he reached the lieutenant the shells hit the beach". The pattern is so (a move), then but (the next blow). Small intensifiers make each blow land faster or harder: "instantly", "far into the air", "unconscious" in place of "lying".

- He prefers events that happen over events that are explained: "where a gunfight brought dozens of soldiers running" became "a gunfight broke out bringing dozens of enemy soldiers running towards them".
- He doesn't spell out motive or payback. He cut "to let Thornton escape", the payback angle I had pushed in chat, and let the action carry it.
- He strips identity down to one bare name: "Navy SEAL Michael Thornton and another SEAL had landed" became "when Michael Thornton landed". He dropped the title and the second man.

- He notices when a key word repeats on nearby lines: "the word lieutenant happens too close together in line one and 2." He wants fixes made inside the existing version: "same version otherwise it gets crowded."

- He writes notes on his craft in brackets inside the script, like "(highest stake in story becomes the hook...)" and "(script ends at the cliffhanger...)". These are lessons for me, not lines to be read aloud.
Mistakes we fixed

- Version 1 was 269 words, full of numbers and names ("about 400 yards", "five miles", "in five minutes", "two-man enemy patrol", "Thomas Norris"). Nick: "can you rewrite this by only taking account my finals?" He wanted his own finals used as the only model for length and detail.

- Version 2 was still too long. I told him it was "about 190 words", but the harness counted 210. I said Version 3 was "about 140", but it was 152. Nick: "isnt it still too long?... usually my script is condensed to 100-150 words." I under-reported my length twice.

- My hook in Versions 1 to 3 was "Navy SEAL Michael Thornton ran back through enemy fire, straight toward the spot his own warship was about to shell." Nick: "even the hook is weak... didnt care about the character at all." He replaced it with "He ran back to the middle of the battlefield to save his lieutenant", which gives the stake and the reason with no name or title, and later added "from enemy gunfire".

- In Version 4 I used "lieutenant" in line 1 and line 2 ("Michael Thornton and his lieutenant had landed"). Nick flagged the repeat. I changed it to "another SEAL", and Nick then cut it further to "when Michael Thornton landed".

- "where a gunfight brought dozens of soldiers running at them" became "a gunfight broke out bringing dozens of enemy soldiers running towards them". He wanted the event to happen, not a relative clause that explains it.
- "and stayed behind to hold the soldiers off to let Thornton escape" lost "to let Thornton escape". The explained motive was cut.

- "only for a bullet to hit him in the head, leaving him lying right where..." became "but instantly got a bullet in the head / leaving him unconscious right where...". The blow is faster and the stake is higher.

- "but Thornton turned around and ran back through the gunfire, shooting the soldiers who were about to reach him" became "so Thornton turned around and ran back through the gunfire". He cut the hero winning a fight because it released tension.
- "and just as he lifted him, the first shells hit" became "but just as he reached the lieutenant the shells hit the beach". The next blow now opens with a "but" turn.

- "throwing both men into the air, yet slowing the soldiers chasing them" became "throwing both men far into the air and giving Thornton time...". He cut the relief beat (the soldiers slowed) and made the blast bigger.

- "strap his lieutenant to his back and swim out to sea, / towing him for two hours until a boat finally found them" was cut down to "swim out to sea escaping from the enemy and finally reaching their boat". Process details were gone.
- I ended on the outcome: "and his lieutenant lived, but lost an eye and part of his skull." He deleted it and ended on the cliffhanger of whether the lieutenant survived, to drive comments.
- Version 4 grew from 152 to 164 words when I added the new hook. I added without cutting elsewhere, so the length went back up.
- When he asked me to look at his version, I listed what he cut. He corrected me: "dont look at just what i cut. look at the flow now. at every moment of the story there is tension."
Rules for next time
- Write 100-150 words, aiming for about 115. Keep a detail only if it raises the danger. Cut distances, times, numbers, titles, second names and how-it-was-done steps (strapping, towing, inflating).

- Line 1 is the story's single highest stake in plain words, with no name or title. It should make the viewer ask "what happens now?" and work as the foreshadow (e.g. "He ran back to the middle of the battlefield to save his lieutenant from enemy gunfire.").
- Every line is either a new threat or a desperate move against one. No relief beats (the hero shoots the attackers, the enemy is slowed, a rescue arrives, it took hours) until the final escape line.
- Chain the lines with turns: "so" for the move, "but" / "but just as..." for the next blow. Use sharp intensifiers on each blow ("instantly", "far into the air", "unconscious").
- End on a cliffhanger. Leave the fate that matters most (did he live?) unsaid so viewers ask in the comments. Don't state the outcome or the motive (no "to let him escape").
- Don't repeat a key noun like "lieutenant" on consecutive lines. Name the hero once, bare ("Michael Thornton"), and drop titles like "Navy SEAL".
- Report word counts exactly the way the harness counts them. I said "about 190" when it was 210 and "about 140" when it was 152. If a version is over 150, say so and cut before sending.
- When Nick asks me to look at his version, explain the flow line by line: what tension each line adds and where mine let it drop. Don't just list what he cut.
- Make small fixes inside the existing version, not as a new one ("same version otherwise it gets crowded"), and confirm the change in one short line.

name: The Invasion Of The Empty Island

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts

Japanese forces held Kiska from 6 June 1942; they attacked a 12-man U.S. Navy weather station, killing two Americans and capturing seven; William C. House escaped and surrendered about 50 days later. [1]
NPS dates the landing to June 7, 1942, when the Third Special Landing Force (550 Japanese naval men) stormed ashore. [2]
After Attu fell on May 30, 1943, Japan planned 'Operation KE' to evacuate Kiska; the garrison destroyed or booby-trapped weapons, equipment and supplies. [2]
On July 28, 1943, two cruisers and six destroyers anchored in Kiska Harbor; in about fifty minutes 5,183 men boarded, without a single loss of life. [2]
Wikipedia gives a differing account: Rear Admiral Kimura Masatomi with two light cruisers and ten destroyers rescued 5,193 men on July 29, 1943 under cover of fog. [1]
Radio signals from Kiska ceased entirely on July 28; the Japanese withdrew under cover of fog while the naval blockade was interrupted for refuelling. [3]
On 27 July 1943 U.S. battleships west of Kiska fired 518 14-inch shells at radar contacts; no Japanese surface warships were within 200 miles. [4]
Bombardment of the island by warships and aircraft continued in the first weeks of August. [3]
The landing began August 15, 1943; listed strength 34,000 U.S. and 5,300 Canadian troops. [3]
A Canadian soldier fired on U.S. lines believing them Japanese; friendly fire killed 28 Americans and 4 Canadians and wounded about 50 on each side. [3]
Friendly fire aided by thick fog killed 24 soldiers; booby traps killed four. [1]

Sherrod called the fog the 'foggiest I have ever seen' with visibility under ten feet; censors blocked his report that about 25 were killed and 31 wounded by friendly fire; a Canadian lieutenant was killed by a booby-trapped radio. [5]
At 0150 on August 18, 1943, USS Abner Read's stern struck a drifting enemy mine off Kiska; 70 missing presumed dead, 1 confirmed dead, 47 wounded. [6]
Allied losses totaled 92 killed and 221 wounded (intro elsewhere says over 500 casualties). [3]
Apart from 'a few stray dogs,' the island was empty when the Allies attacked. [7]
Troops found a few dogs and a container of hot coffee; a pilot joked the dogs couldn't read the 100,000 leaflets dropped. [5]
The dog Explosion, from the U.S. weather station and cared for by the Japanese, was among the dogs that met the Allied troops. [1]
General Simon B. Buckner called it 'a great big, juicy, expensive mistake.' [2]

paragraphs: The Invasion Of The Empty Island
Almost 40,000 American and Canadian soldiers landed on an island and started shooting into fog so thick they couldn't see ten feet ahead.
You see, Japanese troops had stormed the island of Kiska and captured the small American weather station there,
so over a year later, the Americans and Canadians came to take it back,
where a Canadian soldier opened fire, sure the men in front of him were Japanese,
starting a fight in the fog that killed 28 Americans and 4 Canadians,
but there were no Japanese left to fight,

since weeks earlier, when the American ships guarding the island pulled back to refuel, Japanese ships hidden by the fog slipped into the harbor and carried over 5,000 men away in about fifty minutes,
yet even after the island's radio went silent, American warships and planes kept pounding it for weeks,
and as the troops searched the island, all they found were a few dogs and the booby traps the Japanese had left behind, which killed more of them,
so taking an island with no enemy on it cost 92 Allied lives.

name: The Captain Who Saved His Enemies

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts
The engagement was the Second Battle of the Java Sea on 1 March 1942; HMS Exeter sank at 11:40 after a boiler-room hit and two torpedoes from the destroyer Inazuma. [1]

HMS Encounter was immobilised by shell hits and set on fire while laying smoke for Exeter; her captain Eric Morgan ordered her scuttled to prevent capture, and she sank about 12:10. USS Pope was dive-bombed and sunk around 13:50. [1]
The survivors had been adrift for some 20 hours, in rafts and lifejackets or clinging to floats, many coated in oil and unable to see. [2]
One Encounter survivor's log says he was in the water for 24 hours. [3]
The rescue placed Ikazuchi at risk of submarine attack and interfered with her fighting ability due to the sheer numbers of rescued sailors. [2]

Allied submarine and aircraft threats lurked in the area; Kudo posted guards with light machine guns and sent the entire crew except the first turret gunners to the rescue, using rope ladders, bamboo poles, torpedo cranes and ammunition derricks; some castaways sank as they grabbed bamboo poles. [4]
Ikazuchi had about 220 crew against roughly 500 castaways. [4]
Ikazuchi's record notes she rescued 404 men from HMS Exeter and Encounter on 2 March and another 18 at a different moment; on 1-3 March she carried crew to Bandjermasin and unloaded prisoners. [5]
Kudo's Wikipedia article instead says he ordered Ikazuchi to rescue 442 survivors from HMS Encounter and USS Pope on 2 March 1942. [2]
Ikazuchi's Wikipedia article says she rescued the remaining 400-odd survivors from Exeter and Encounter on 2 March 1942. [6]
Japanese sailors wiped the oil-covered survivors with cotton, alcohol, petrol and fresh water, gave or made clothes, and distributed milk, beer and dry bread. [4]

Kudo told the British officers in English: 'You have fought bravely. Now you are the honoured guests of the Imperial Japanese Navy,' and added, 'I respect the English Navy, but your government is foolish to make war on Japan.' [4]
The hospital ship Op Ten Noort was escorted to Banjarmasin and embarked 970 POWs, about 800 of whom were Exeter survivors; no source read confirms a next-day handover from Ikazuchi. [7]
Op Ten Noort did not depart for Makassar until 8 March 1942. [8]
Encounter's survivors spent three and a half years of captivity in Macassar on Celebes. [9]
Just over 800 survivors of the three ships were imprisoned by the Japanese, and 190 died in captivity. [1]
Ikazuchi was torpedoed and sunk by USS Harder on 13 April 1944 with no survivors. [6]
Kudo left the navy after the war, moved to Kawaguchi, Saitama, and died of stomach cancer on 12 January 1979, aged 78. [2]

Sam Falle (1919-2014) spent three and a half years as a POW, later became a diplomat, sought out Kudo's grave and visited it on 7 December 2008; Kudo's family learned of the rescue for the first time when Falle visited. [10]
In 2003 Falle asked author Ryunosuke Megumi to find Kudo; in 2008, against medical advice, he tried to stand from his wheelchair at Kudo's grave. Kudo had never told anyone, including his family. [4]

Japanese captain Shunsaku Kudo stopped his warship in waters where enemy submarines and planes were lurking, beside hundreds of British and American sailors his own navy had sunk the day before,
because they had been drifting for about 20 hours, clinging to rafts and floats, many so coated in oil they couldn't see,
and since he respected the British navy, he couldn't leave them there,
so he sent almost his whole crew to pull them aboard with rope ladders and bamboo poles, keeping only the gunners of his front turret ready to fight,
until his ship was carrying more than 400 enemy sailors against his own crew of about 220, too crowded to fight back if a submarine struck,
where Kudo told the British officers in English, 'You have fought bravely. Now you are the honoured guests of the Imperial Japanese Navy,'
but he never spoke of it to anyone, not even his family,
so they only learned what he had done after he died, when one of the men he had saved came looking for his grave.

name: The Pig That Almost Started A War

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts
On June 15, 1859, American settler Lyman Cutlar shot and killed a Hudson's Bay Company pig rooting in his garden. [1]
The pig belonged to Charles Griffin, manager for the Hudson's Bay Company; it was rooting for potatoes in Cutlar's garden. [2]
Cutlar offered $10 for the pig; Griffin demanded $100; Cutlar then refused to pay, saying the pig had been trespassing. The 'eating my potatoes' exchange is described as likely apocryphal. [3]
Griffin demanded '$100 for a $10 pig' and threatened to evict Cutlar and other Americans. [4]
British authorities threatened to arrest Cutlar and evict all Americans as trespassers; settlers asked Brig. Gen. William S. Harney for military protection. [1]
Wikipedia's claim that British authorities threatened to arrest Cutlar is tagged 'citation needed'. [3]
Capt. George E. Pickett and Company D, 9th U.S. Infantry, landed on San Juan Island on July 27, 1859, with 64 men. [1]
Harney sent 66 men under Pickett, who said he would 'fight to the last man' if attacked. [2]

Governor James Douglas ordered Capt. Geoffrey Phipps Hornby to remove Pickett without an armed clash if possible; Hornby commanded HMS Tribune (31-gun frigate), joined by HMS Satellite and HMS Plumper. [1]
Hornby refused to act until Rear Admiral Robert L. Baynes arrived. [3]

On August 10 Lt. Col. Silas Casey reinforced Pickett with 171 men; by August 31 about 461 Americans with 14 field cannons were encamped, plus eight 32-pounder naval guns in a redoubt; the British had 52 guns in total. [1]
By August 10, 1859, the Americans had 461 men and 14 cannons under Casey; the British had five warships with 70 guns and 2,140 men. [3]
By the end of August, 461 American soldiers and 14 cannons faced five British warships carrying 167 guns and 2,140 troops. [2]
Rear Adm. Baynes refused to escalate, saying he would not 'involve two great nations in a war over a squabble about a pig.' [1]
President Buchanan sent Gen. Winfield Scott, who arranged for both sides to withdraw most forces in October; in November both nations approved joint military occupation; Harney was rebuked. [1]
Joint occupation was limited to token forces of no more than 100 men each. [3]
British Royal Marines established English Camp at Garrison Bay on March 21, 1860. [1]

The joint occupation lasted 12 years. The 1871 Treaty of Washington referred the dispute to Kaiser Wilhelm I, who assigned a three-man commission; after nearly a year in Geneva it ruled for the U.S. on October 21, 1872, setting the boundary through Haro Strait. [1]
Royal Marines left English Camp on November 25, 1872; the last U.S. troops left American Camp by July 1874. [1]
The only casualty was the pig. [1]

tabs.title: Learnings
paragraphs: What "The Pig That Almost Started A War" taught me
What I learned

- Nick's cut for this script is about 141 words, down from my versions at 199, 196 and 167. He said "there was still quite a bit of fluff and unneccessary details in this one too, but the flow was great". My first drafts are too long even when the flow is good, and the next script got the same note ("too long, cut the fluff, keep the flow intact").

- To Nick, fluff means facts that pile up: prices ($10 / $100), the trespassing excuse, "a captain and dozens of", and the troop maths ("461 American soldiers with 14 cannons faced 5 British warships carrying over 2,000 men"). He cut the numbers line in three passes: first the cannons, then the 461, then the whole line.

- I got wrong which lines were fluff. I offered to cut "who swore to fight to the last man if attacked" and "putting both sides one order away from war". He kept both and cut the numbers instead. Stakes lines and vivid quotes are flow to him. Lists of details are fluff.

- He wants the conflict in the first two lines. His opening puts the pig's owner in the hook ("a pig that belonged to a British company") and the threat in line 2 ("But when the farmer refused to pay for it the British threatened to arrest him"). He skips the back-and-forth over the price completely.

- He keeps the tone plain and uses general groups ("the British", "soldiers"), not side characters with titles (manager, captain). The only role he kept is the admiral, because the admiral delivers the punchline quote.

- He found the story funny ("this is pretty funny") and asked which island it was. I suggested putting "on San Juan Island" back in the hook, and he didn't. Him being curious about a fact doesn't mean he wants it in the script.

- He changed the hook's full stop to a comma ("potatoes,") and left "But" with a capital letter. I don't know if that was on purpose. I shouldn't build a rule on it, and I should ask if it ever matters for the harness.

- I said wrongly that there were no comments. He asked "did i make any comments on the doc recently?" and I said I couldn't see any, but there was one ("csjdokdsnc", on the admiral line). It looks like test text, but my answer was wrong all the same.
Mistakes we fixed

- Opening, Version 2: "You see, the pig belonged to a British company, and when the farmer offered $10 for it, the company's manager demanded $100, / but the farmer refused to pay anything, saying the pig had been trespassing, so the British threatened to arrest him," was changed to "An American farmer shot a pig that belonged to a British company when it was caught digging up his potatoes, / But when the farmer refused to pay for it the British threatened to arrest him,". The owner moves into the hook, the haggling and the excuse go, and the threat arrives in line 2.

- Hook: "An American farmer living on an island claimed by both America and Britain shot a pig..." lost the island clause. A later line already says "an island it claimed", so the hook was repeating it.

- "which sent a captain and dozens of soldiers, who swore to fight to the last man if attacked" became "which sent soldiers who swore to fight to the last man if attacked". The captain has no name or job later in the story, so he was extra.

- "while America kept bringing in more troops until 461 American soldiers with 14 cannons faced 5 British warships carrying over 2,000 men," was deleted completely, in three steps: cannons, then the number, then the line. The escalation still works without a pile of numbers.
- "it sent warships to remove them" became "it then sent warships to remove them". The added "then" smooths the order of events once the troops line was gone.

- I had the cuts wrong: I suggested cutting "who swore to fight to the last man" and "one order away from war", and he kept both. My first version also had "the British captain waited for his admiral to arrive and decide". I cut that myself in Version 2 and he agreed it should go.
Rules for next time
- Put the conflict in the first two lines. The hook says who did what and who it belonged to, and line 2 is the threat. Skip the haggling, prices and excuses.
- Cut piles of numbers like troop counts, cannons, ships and men. Keep at most one number, and only if it's simple and pays off, like "12 years".
- Keep the lines that show stakes and voice ("fight to the last man", "one order away from war", the punchline quote). The fluff to cut is details, not those lines.
- Refer to groups ("the British", "soldiers"), not side characters with titles. Only name a role, like the admiral, when that person gets a quote or a decision.
- Don't put a setting detail in the hook if a later line already gives it. Leave out place names unless the story needs them.
- Aim for about 140 words on the first draft. My versions here were 199, 196 and 167, and his final was about 141.
- When Nick asks if the fluff is cut, or asks me to cut it, make the cuts in a new version and list what went. Don't answer "I can strike them if you want" or ask for permission twice.
- When he asks me to do something ("compare the two scripts and start writing what you learnt"), do it then and there. Don't reply by asking where to put it.
- Before telling him what's in the doc, check every comment thread. I missed his comment on the admiral line and told him there were none.

name: No Shooting On Christmas Eve

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts
On Christmas Eve 1944, Fritz Vincken (12) and his mother Elisabeth were in an isolated cabin in the Hürtgen Forest near the Belgian border during the Battle of the Bulge. [1]
Three armed American soldiers came to the door; two were standing and the third lay severely wounded in the snow. Elisabeth let them in; Fritz wrote he was 'almost paralyzed with fear.' [1]
In Fritz's account the Americans were Jim, Robin and Harry; Harry had been shot in the upper leg, and his mother treated their frostbitten feet and fingers. [2]
Harboring the enemy was punishable by death. [3]
Fritz knew sheltering enemy soldiers counted as treason and could mean execution for everyone in the house. [2]
Four German soldiers separated from their unit asked for shelter; Elisabeth told the objecting corporal, 'It is the Holy Night and there will be no shooting here.' [1]
Fritz's account calls the German leader a sergeant and quotes his mother: 'in this Holy Night we do not think of killing.' [2]
The Germans put two pistols, three carbines, a light machine gun and two bazookas on the woodpile; the Americans gave up their weapons too. [2]
A German who had studied medicine in Heidelberg found Harry's wound uninfected because of the cold and said he 'simply needs rest and nourishing meals.' [2]
The rooster Hermann was not enough for everyone, so Elisabeth made chicken soup with potatoes and oats; the German corporal added red wine and rye bread; she said grace and some soldiers wept. [1]

The next morning, after a stretcher was made from two sticks and her best tablecloth, the German sergeant used Jim's map to show the Americans the way to their troops; she returned the weapons, and the men shook hands and left in opposite directions. [2]
The Germans gave the Americans a compass; in 1996 Ralph Blank still had the German compass and map. [3]
Reagan told the story at Bitburg Air Base on May 5, 1985: 'The woman was afraid, but she quickly said with a firm voice, There will be no shooting here.' [4]

After a 1995 Unsolved Mysteries segment, a chaplain in Frederick, Md., contacted the show about Ralph Blank, an 8th Infantry Division sergeant; in 1996 Fritz met Blank, then 76 and in poor health, who told him 'Your mother saved my life.' [1]
Blank died in 1999 at 79 and Fritz in 2001 at 69; Hubert died in 1963 and Elisabeth in 1966. [2]
DVIDS gives Fritz Vincken's death date as Dec. 2, 2002, and says he found one other American but could not contact any of the Germans. [3]

[2] https://battleofthebulge.org/?p=9450
[3] https://www.dvidshub.net/news/436015/o-silent-night
[4] https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/research/speeches/50585b

paragraphs: No Shooting On Christmas Eve
I was a 12-year-old German boy hiding with my mother in a cabin ~~deep in the forest near the Belgian border~~ **in the forest** , while one of the biggest battles of the war raged around us.
And on Christmas Eve, when three armed American soldiers knocked on our door, one of them shot in the leg ~~and lying in the snow~~ , my mother let them in.
But I was ~~almost paralyzed with fear~~ **terrified** , because hiding enemy soldiers counted as treason, and it could get ~~everyone in our house~~ **us all**  executed.
Then, while she was treating ~~their frozen feet and fingers~~ **them** , there was another knock.
It was four German soldiers ~~who had lost their unit and were asking~~ **lost and asking**  for shelter.
And the moment they ~~stepped inside and~~  saw the Americans, their leader started to object.
But my mother looked at him and said, 'It is the Holy Night, and there will be no shooting here.'

So the Germans ~~piled their pistols, rifles, a machine gun and two bazookas on the woodpile, the Americans gave up their weapons too,~~ **laid down their weapons, the Americans did the same,**  and one of the Germans, who had studied medicine, checked the wounded American's leg ~~and found the cold had kept it from getting infected~~ .

Since our one rooster wasn't enough to feed everyone, my mother cooked it into a soup ~~with potatoes and oats, the Germans added red wine and bread,~~  and when she said grace, some of the soldiers cried.

The next morning, ~~after my mother gave up her best tablecloth to make a stretcher,~~  the German leader used the Americans' map to show them the way back to their troops, gave them a compass, ~~and once my mother handed back everyone's weapons,~~  they shook hands and walked off in opposite directions.
For the next 50 years, I had no idea if any of those soldiers made it home.

But after a TV show told our story, ~~a chaplain in America called in about an old soldier named Ralph Blank, and when I finally met him, he was 76 and sick,~~ **I finally met one of the Americans, who**  still had the German compass and map, and told me ~~five~~ **four**  words.
Your mother saved my life.
My mother never got to hear it, because she had died 30 years earlier.

name: The Captain Who Sank His Own Ship

tabs.title: Fun Facts
paragraphs: Fun Facts
Over about 10 weeks Langsdorff stopped and sank nine British merchant ships of over 50,000 tons, avoided killing anyone and followed the Hague Conventions. [1]
Captured crews respected him because he welcomed them aboard, saluted them and apologised for sinking their ships; he sank nine ships without any loss of life. [2]
On 15 November 1939 Graf Spee stopped Africa Shell in the Mozambique Channel; the crew were allowed to row for shore, but Captain Dove was taken prisoner and became friendly with Langsdorff. [3]
Clement's crew took to their lifeboats and reached the Brazilian coast; other prisoners were moved to the supply ship Altmark. [4]

Battle of 13 December 1939 against Exeter, Ajax and Achilles under Commodore Harwood: Exeter had 61 dead; Graf Spee was hit about 70 times, with 36 killed and 60 wounded, Langsdorff among the wounded. [4]
Langsdorff asked Uruguay for two weeks and was told he could not stay beyond 72 hours; the British also had merchant ships sail at 24-hour intervals, using a Hague rule to hold him in port. [5]
Uruguay required him to leave by 20:00 on 17 December 1939 or be interned. [1]
Prisoners still aboard were released when the ship arrived in Montevideo (around 00:10 on 14 December); prisoners on Altmark were freed by HMS Cossack in February 1940. [5]
61 prisoners were released: 6 captains, 9 chief engineers, 25 officers and 21 seamen. [4]

British signals sent on frequencies German intelligence was known to intercept suggested a large force including Ark Royal and Renown was gathering; in fact only Cumberland had arrived (22:00, 14 December), and the real reinforcements would not gather until 19 December. [5]
Ark Royal and Renown were about 2,500 nautical miles away. [4]

Langsdorff ordered the scuttling at 20:55 on 17 December with about 40 men aboard; he wanted to save his crew and also to avoid internment that could give British intelligence access to the ship; about 20,000 people watched and an Argentine tug took off the crew. [4]
Langsdorff is quoted as saying 'Rather 1 000 live young men, than 1 000 dead young heroes'; Hitler had ordered the ship must not be interned and did not approve of the scuttling. [2]
Langsdorff shot himself on 20 December 1939 in a Buenos Aires hotel room, in full dress uniform, lying on the ship's battle ensign. [4]
His farewell letter is dated 19 December and takes sole responsibility for the scuttling; the historian Dudley Pope, cited on the page, identifies the flag as an Imperial naval ensign. [1]

At the 15 December Montevideo funeral for Graf Spee's battle dead, several British merchant captains who had been prisoners aboard laid a wreath 'To the memory of brave men of the sea from their comrades of the British Merchant Service'; Langsdorff was buried at La Chacarita, Buenos Aires, on 21 December with full honours. [6]
Langsdorff was buried in Buenos Aires with full military honours, and several British officers attended. [5]
The British sent a wreath inscribed 'To the brave German Captain' for Langsdorff's funeral. [2]

paragraphs: The Captain Who Sank His Own Ship

~~A German captain sank nine British cargo ships without killing a single person, and whenever he took a crew prisoner, he welcomed them aboard his warship, saluted them and apologized for sinking their ship.~~
~~That is, until three British warships caught up with him and hit his ship about 70 times, wounding him too, which sent him limping into a port in Uruguay, a country that stayed out of the war,~~

~~where he was told he had only 72 hours to leave, while the British, knowing the Germans listened to their radio, sent fake messages that a huge fleet with an aircraft carrier was waiting outside, when really only one more ship had arrived,~~
~~So instead of leading his men into a fight he was sure they would lose, he decided to sink his own ship, saying he would rather have a thousand young men alive than a thousand dead heroes,~~
~~and with 20,000 people watching from the shore, explosives tore the ship apart and it sank,~~
~~yet not one of his sailors died, because a tug had already carried them all away,~~
~~But three days later, he put on his full dress uniform, lay down on his ship's battle flag and shot himself, leaving a letter that took all the blame for the sinking,~~
~~And when he was buried with full military honors,~~
~~the British, whose ships he had sunk, sent a wreath that read 'To the brave German Captain.'~~
**My version**
A German captain sank nine British cargo ships without killing a single person, and whenever he took a crew prisoner, he welcomed them and apologized for sinking their ship.

But when some British warships hit his ship about 70 times, he ended up limping into a port in Uruguay, where he was told he had only 72 hours to leave, **while the British sent fake radio messages**  that a huge fleet with an aircraft carrier was waiting outside to seize his ship but since **it carried Germany's secret new radar**  there was no way he would let them take it**,**
So instead of giving up his country’s secrets he detonated **explosives he had planted on board,**  which tore the ship apart**,**
**And since** **he couldn't bear anyone thinking he sank his ship to save his own life, three days later he shot himself .**

tabs.title: Learnings
paragraphs: What "The Captain Who Sank His Own Ship" taught me
What I learned

- Nick checks the logic of each line by asking why it's there. He asked "what is the reason for this?" about the radio-trick line and "why did he have to sink his ship?" about the sinking line. If a line doesn't say how it pushes the captain toward what he does next, he stops and asks. Nothing is allowed to be just background.

- He wants one reason running through the whole story, and it should be the hero's own. He chose protecting the secrets over saving the crew: "i think its more important that he was willing to protect his country's secrets than the crew". His version turns every beat toward the secrets: the fleet is waiting "to seize his ship", "there was no way he would let them take it", "instead of giving up his country's secrets".

- He cuts any person the viewer hasn't met: "added new people into the story that we dont know about or care about them. it just confuses people." The crew, the tug, the 20,000 people watching and the British at the funeral were all cut. Places that set the scene are fine: "uruguay was a good addition."

- He sees ceremony and pictures as fluff. He cut "aboard his warship, saluted them", "wounding him too", "a country that stayed out of the war" and the 20,000 people watching. He also cut the full dress uniform and battle flag: "isnt this fluff who cares about this?"

- He wants the ending to hurt, and for him that comes from the reason, not the details. He said "this captain was portrayed. a hero so we care about him and the sad ending doesn't make me feel it fully". He kept the motive clause and ended on the bare act: "three days later he shot himself".

- He cuts hard. The bot's 9 lines and 241 words became 4 lines of about 145 words, in one chain held together by commas. He dropped the whole wreath ending from the approved script this one was built on. That callback mattered less to him than a short, sharp finish.

- He likes to write the draft himself and then ask for review: "let me finish the script and you can go over it and see what i changed". He welcomes small, precise fixes ("your recommendations where perfect") and takes them on one by one. Big rewrites he handles himself.

- He guards his text closely. Anything turning up in the doc that he didn't ask for reads to him as an edit made without permission. When he got frustrated he swore in Greeklish ("gamo tin mana su"). He also has little patience for confusing tool features, like the auto-checker's "To fix" cards and dark-mode formatting coming along when he pasted.

paragraphs: The King Who Ate Poison
He swallowed a little poison every single day for years, and it ruined the last moment of his life.
You see, when King Mithridates was a boy, his father was poisoned at dinner,
so, sure he'd be next, he started swallowing tiny doses of poison until his body could survive it,
keeping it up as king through decades of war with Rome,
but when he finally lost, he ordered his exhausted army to march on Italy,
and his own son, sure this would kill them all, turned the soldiers against him,
trapping him in his fortress,
where, rather than be paraded through Rome in chains, he took out the poison he carried,
sharing it with his two daughters, who begged to drink first and died within moments,
only for his own body to fight it off,
forcing the man who had beaten poison to beg his own bodyguard to kill him with a sword.

tabs.title: What Makes The Next Script Better
paragraphs: Make the viewer care about the character: pick the moments with emotional weight over neutral facts.
Every connective must be true: "so" needs a real cause and "but" a real contrast. If it isn't true, rewrite the line, don't swap the word.
Write it as one long sentence chained by connectives, and never repeat a connective close to itself.
Each action must cause the next. Pick the action that makes what follows inevitable: overpowering the guards leads to gunfire, forcing a door doesn't.
Give anyone or anything a reason to be in the story before it acts. Never first name a power after it has already won.
Give every betrayal and big decision its why, because that is where the drama is.
Say plainly who does what. No dangling fragments that leave the listener unsure what is happening.
Every word must add to the story. Cut emphasis words, redundant words, and true details that make the listener stop and puzzle.
Use words a viewer gets the first time they hear them. If a term needs a second of thought, replace it.
One story, one topic. Cut anything that starts a second story.
When how it happened is the interesting part, spend a line showing how.
On a rewrite, use the writer's exact wording and change only what they marked and what the lines beside it need.

Make sure every step physically follows from the one before it.
